items.stem: The chart shows U.S. manufacturing employment (millions of workers) at selected years. Which claim about the American economy between 1979 and 2000 is best supported by the data?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Manufacturing Employment, 1979–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures consistent with the manufacturing job losses of the globalization era described in u9.md §The story (NAFTA, WTO, tech boom) and §What the exam tests here (who gained, who lost under globalization).

options: (A) Manufacturing employment never recovered to its 1979 peak during these years.
(B) Manufacturing employment grew steadily across the entire period.
(C) The data show that NAFTA caused the decline in manufacturing jobs.
(D) Automation had no effect on manufacturing employment levels.
items.explanation: The chart shows 19.4 million manufacturing workers in 1979, the highest value plotted, with every later year lower — so the peak was never regained. The chart records employment levels, not causes, so it cannot by itself prove what drove the decline.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 1979 value of 19.4 million is the highest on the chart, and the 1983, 1989, 1993, and 2000 values are all lower, so the claim follows directly from the data.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The line falls from 19.4 million in 1979 to 16.7 million in 1983 and stays below the 1979 peak in every later year shown; that is not steady growth.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The chart shows when employment fell, not why. The decline was already underway by 1983, a decade before NAFTA took effect in 1994, and a single time series cannot isolate one cause.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart shows head counts, not output per worker or the reasons plants closed; it provides no evidence about automation's role either way.

items.stem: During the late twentieth century, the Sun Belt grew rapidly in population and jobs while many Rust Belt cities lost both. Which development best explains the Sun Belt's growth?
options: (A) Sun Belt states outlawed all factory construction to keep their air clean, which attracted tourists instead of industry.
(B) Lower taxes, lower labor costs, air conditioning, and defense and aerospace spending drew businesses and migrants south and west.
(C) The federal government moved every military base out of the Northeast as punishment for high union membership.
(D) Sun Belt growth came entirely from retirees, with no new businesses or working-age migrants involved.
items.explanation: The Sun Belt's rise combined business-friendly tax and labor conditions, the spread of air conditioning, and large federal defense and aerospace investments. Firms and workers moved toward those advantages while older industrial centers in the Northeast and Midwest — the Rust Belt — lost factories and population.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Sun Belt states courted industry rather than banning it; new factories, offices, and suburbs were central to the region's growth.
option_explanations.B: Correct. These were the main pull factors: lower operating costs for firms, a comfortable climate made livable year-round by air conditioning, and federal military and space spending concentrated in the South and West.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Base locations reflected strategy and politics, not a coordinated punishment of unionized states, and many Northern bases remained open.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Retirees were one part of Sun Belt migration, but the larger story was working-age migrants and relocating employers seeking lower costs.

items.stem: Beginning in the 1980s and accelerating after NAFTA took effect in 1994, many American companies moved production to Mexico and Asia. Which combination of factors best explains this offshoring?
options: (A) American consumers stopped buying manufactured goods, so factories had no reason to stay open anywhere.
(B) U.S. law required companies to manufacture abroad once they reached a certain size.
(C) Lower wages abroad, trade agreements that cut tariffs, and containerized shipping made overseas production cheaper than domestic production.
(D) Foreign governments paid American companies to close their U.S. plants and leave the workers unemployed.
items.explanation: Offshoring was a cost decision. Trade deals such as NAFTA lowered the tariff barriers that had protected domestic production, container ships made long-distance transport cheap, and much lower wages abroad made it profitable to move assembly overseas even after shipping costs.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Americans kept buying manufactured goods in growing quantities; what changed was where those goods were made, with imports filling the gap.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. No such law existed. Companies moved production voluntarily to cut costs, responding to market incentives and trade policy, not to a legal mandate.
option_explanations.C: Correct. These three conditions together — cheap foreign labor, lower trade barriers, and cheap ocean freight — made producing abroad and shipping back to U.S. consumers the profitable choice.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Foreign governments offered tax breaks and infrastructure to attract investment, but they did not pay firms to close American plants; the decision was driven by the firms' own cost calculations.

items.stem: When air-traffic controllers struck in 1981, President Reagan fired them — what the review calls 'a landmark defeat for organized labor.' The chart shows union membership as a share of U.S. workers, 1980–2020. Which claim is best supported by combining the chart with that event?

chart_spec.title: Union Membership as Share of U.S. Workers, 1980–2020
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the steady decline follows the PATCO turning point described in u9.md §Key terms (PATCO strike, 1981, 'a landmark defeat for organized labor').

options: (A) Union membership rose after 1981 because the PATCO firings inspired a wave of new organizing.
(B) The chart proves that the PATCO firings were the sole cause of union decline.
(C) Union decline stopped in 2000 and membership recovered most of its losses by 2020.
(D) Union density fell by roughly a third between 1980 and 2000, a decline for which PATCO was a landmark event but not the only cause.
items.explanation: The chart shows union density falling from about 20 percent in 1980 to about 13.5 percent in 2000 — roughly a one-third drop — and continuing down to 2020. PATCO signaled that employers and government would confront strikes aggressively, but the decline also reflected factory closures, the shift to service jobs, and employer resistance, so no single event explains the whole trend.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows membership falling, not rising, in the years right after 1981, from 20.1 percent in 1980 to 18.0 percent in 1985.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The chart is a time series of membership levels; it shows that decline happened, but it cannot prove that one event caused all of it. Historians cite several causes working together.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The 2020 value of 10.8 percent is lower than the 2000 value of 13.5 percent, so the decline continued rather than reversing.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The math fits the chart (20.1 to 13.5 is about a one-third fall), and the review presents PATCO as a landmark defeat — a turning point within a broader decline, not its sole cause.

items.stem: By the 1990s, service-sector jobs — in health care, retail, finance, restaurants, and technology — made up a growing share of American employment while manufacturing's share shrank. Historians describe this shift as which of the following?
options: (A) A structural change from an industrial economy toward a post-industrial, service-based economy.
(B) A temporary effect of the 1990–91 recession that reversed itself by the end of the decade.
(C) The result of a federal law banning the construction of new factories after 1985.
(D) Evidence that Americans had largely stopped buying manufactured goods.
items.explanation: The move from factory work to service work was a long-term restructuring of the economy, not a passing cycle. Manufacturing output remained high, but employment shifted toward services as production moved abroad and automation reduced factory head counts.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Economists call this the post-industrial transition: the economy's center of employment moved from making goods to providing services, a structural change that persisted across business cycles.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The service share of employment kept growing through the booming late 1990s, so the shift was not a recession artifact that reversed.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No such law existed; factories continued to be built in the United States, especially in the South, even as total manufacturing employment fell.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. American consumption of manufactured goods grew; the change was in where goods were produced, with imports supplying much of the demand.

items.stem: The review notes that the Reagan-era recovery brought 'huge deficits and stark inequality.' Which mechanism best connects deindustrialization to the rise in inequality?
options: (A) Factory workers retired early in large numbers and stopped spending money, which impoverished their towns.
(B) High-wage, unionized manufacturing jobs were replaced by lower-wage service jobs, widening the gap between top and middle incomes.
(C) The federal government raised taxes on wealthy Americans to the highest rates in the nation's history.
(D) Inequality rose because the overall U.S. population shrank, leaving fewer workers to share the national income.
items.explanation: Unionized factory jobs had paid middle-class wages with benefits. When those jobs disappeared and were replaced by lower-paying retail, food-service, and other service work, workers in the middle of the income distribution fell behind while highly educated professionals and investors pulled ahead.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Early retirement was not the main story; the issue was that the jobs replacing factory work paid less, not that workers stopped spending.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The wage gap between a unionized auto or steel job and a typical service job was large, and millions of workers made exactly that downward move, stretching the income distribution.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Federal tax policy in this era cut top rates rather than raising them; tax changes did not compress incomes.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The U.S. population grew throughout this period, and a shrinking population would not by itself widen the gap between rich and poor.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reaganomics brought 'huge deficits and stark inequality'

items.stem: Based on the chart of U.S. manufacturing employment, 1979–2000, alone, which conclusion is warranted?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Manufacturing Employment, 1979–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures consistent with the manufacturing job losses of the globalization era described in u9.md §The story and §What the exam tests here.

options: (A) NAFTA destroyed exactly 1.2 million manufacturing jobs.
(B) Factory workers were happier in 2000 than they had been in 1979.
(C) Manufacturing employment in 2000 was lower than it had been in 1979.
(D) The 1983 dip was caused by the PATCO strike of 1981.
items.explanation: The chart directly compares two plotted values: 17.3 million in 2000 against 19.4 million in 1979, so the later figure was lower. The chart records employment levels only, so it cannot establish what caused any of the changes it shows.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows total employment, not jobs lost to a single cause, and it cannot produce an exact figure for NAFTA's effect; the decline was already underway a decade before NAFTA took effect.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The chart contains no information about workers' attitudes or well-being, only head counts.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Both values are plotted on the chart, and 17.3 million is less than 19.4 million — a direct reading of the data with no inference about causes required.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart shows when employment fell, not why; PATCO involved air-traffic controllers rather than factory workers, and the dip coincided with the deep 1981–82 recession as well.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — PATCO strike (1981); §The story — globalization-era restructuring

items.stem: The review asks students to compare late-1800s industrial globalization with post-1990 globalization. Which statement makes a valid comparison of the two waves?
options: (A) Both waves were driven mainly by American foreign-aid programs that paid other countries to industrialize.
(B) The earlier wave centered on service industries while the later wave centered on steel and railroads.
(C) The earlier wave built American factories to serve domestic markets, while the later wave closed many of those factories to serve American consumers from abroad.

(D) Both waves integrated markets across borders, but the post-1990 wave moved production itself abroad through multinational supply chains, while the earlier wave mainly moved raw materials in and finished goods out.
items.explanation: Both eras saw goods, capital, and labor crossing borders. The difference is in production: the Gilded Age built factories inside the United States to exploit its resources and markets, while the post-1990 era saw American firms split production across countries, hollowing out domestic manufacturing employment even as trade volumes grew.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Foreign aid was a Cold War instrument, not the engine of either globalization wave; private investment and trade drove both.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the two eras: steel and railroads defined the late 1800s, while services and electronics defined the later wave.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Although it gestures at a real contrast, it misstates the earlier wave, which was deeply tied to export markets and foreign capital, not purely domestic demand.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies the genuine continuity (cross-border market integration) and the genuine change (the offshoring of production itself through global supply chains), which is why the later wave displaced American factory workers.

items.stem: The chart shows the federal budget balance from 1980 to 2000, in billions of dollars (negative values are surpluses). Which statement best explains the pattern shown?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; Reagan-era deficits and Clinton-era surpluses per u9.md §The story ('Growth did return, but so did huge deficits'; Clinton 'presided over budget surpluses').

options: (A) Large tax cuts combined with a major military buildup produced big deficits in the 1980s; later, tax increases, spending restraint, and strong growth produced surpluses by the late 1990s.
(B) The deficit disappeared because the federal government stopped all defense spending after the Cold War ended.
(C) The late-1990s surpluses came mainly from cutting Social Security benefits roughly in half.
(D) The chart shows that tax cuts always pay for themselves through faster economic growth.
items.explanation: Reagan cut taxes in 1981 while sharply increasing defense spending, and domestic cuts did not close the gap, so deficits soared — exactly what supply-side critics predicted. In the 1990s, the 1990 and 1993 budget deals raised taxes and restrained spending, and the tech-boom economy swelled revenues, producing the surpluses Clinton presided over.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It matches the chart's two phases: deep deficits through the early 1990s, then a swing to surplus by 1998–2000, and it names the policies behind each phase.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Defense spending fell after the Cold War but remained enormous; the surplus came from higher revenues and budget deals, not from abolishing the military budget.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Social Security benefits were not cut in half; the surplus rested on tax policy, spending caps, and a booming economy.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart contradicts this reading of supply-side theory: the 1981 tax cuts were followed by the largest peacetime deficits to that point, not by self-financing growth.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'Growth did return, but so did huge deficits'; Clinton 'presided over budget surpluses'; §Key terms — Reaganomics

items.stem: The review describes the 1990s as a 'victory lap' featuring 'the longest expansion on record to that point,' driven by personal computers and then the internet. The tech boom is best understood as which of the following?
options: (A) A federal jobs program that hired millions of workers directly into government technology offices.
(B) A new general-purpose technology that raised productivity across the economy, much as railroads and electricity had in earlier eras.
(C) A purely financial bubble with no effect on real production or productivity.
(D) A regional event confined to California that left the national economy untouched.
items.explanation: Computers and the internet changed how nearly every industry operated — communications, retail, finance, manufacturing logistics — lifting productivity growth in the late 1990s. Like earlier general-purpose technologies, the effects spread far beyond the firms that built the technology itself.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The boom was driven by private firms and investment, not by direct federal hiring; government funded some underlying research, but the expansion was a private-sector phenomenon.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The comparison fits: railroads reorganized nineteenth-century commerce and electricity reorganized twentieth-century factories, and information technology reorganized late-twentieth-century work.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. A speculative bubble did inflate around dot-com stocks, but beneath it real productivity gains occurred as businesses adopted computing throughout the economy.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. California was a center, but technology investment and adoption spread nationally, and the expansion lifted employment and incomes across the country.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'the tech boom — personal computers, then the internet — delivered the longest expansion on record to that point'
